questions.question: Compare ES modules and CommonJS. What do importers actually receive in each system, and why does that matter?
questions.answer:
ESM uses static import/export declarations, builds an asynchronous module graph, and gives importers live read-only bindings. If the exporting module changes an exported let, every importer sees the new value. ESM also supports top-level await, has top-level this === undefined, is always strict, and can be tree-shaken because imports are static.

CommonJS uses synchronous require and module.exports. require returns the exported object, and destructuring copies values at require time, so a later change to a primitive export is not visible to the importer. Modules are cached by resolved filename, so repeated requires return the same object and the module body runs once. CommonJS has no top-level await and top-level this is module.exports. Use ESM for new code and browser output; expect CommonJS in older Node packages and config files.
key_points: ESM exports live bindings; CJS copies values at require time
ESM is async/static; CJS is synchronous and cached
ESM has top-level await and strict mode by default
CJS module body runs once per resolved filename

questions.question: What changes when you add type="module" to a script tag? Mention scope, timing, strict mode, and top-level this.
questions.answer:
A classic script runs in the global scope, so its top-level var and function declarations become properties of window, and it blocks HTML parsing while it loads and executes. Its top-level this is window, and strict mode is opt-in.

With type="module", the file gets its own module scope: top-level declarations are private unless exported, so two modules can reuse the same names. Modules are strict by default, deferred until parsing finishes, and evaluated once even if included multiple times. Top-level this is undefined. Imports must come from a server with a JavaScript MIME type; file:// pages are usually blocked by CORS. A module can import other modules, use import.meta, and use top-level await.
key_points: Classic scripts share global scope; modules are file-scoped
Modules are strict and deferred by default
Module top-level this is undefined, not window
Modules evaluate once and require a proper MIME type

questions.answer:
It prints 1 0.

The imported count is a live binding: the module namespace points at the exporting module's variable, so after increment() runs, reading count gives 1. snapshot is a separate const initialised with the value at that moment, so it stays 0. This is not destructuring of an object — ESM imports are references to bindings.

CommonJS behaves differently: const { count } = require("./counter") copies the number at require time, so the same code would print 0 0. Imported bindings are also read-only: assigning count = 5 from the importer throws a TypeError. To mutate module state, export a function that does it.
key_points: ESM imports are live read-only bindings
A local const snapshot is copied once
CJS destructuring copies the value at require time
Mutate state through exported functions

questions.answer:
It logs loaded once, then true prod.

require caches modules by resolved filename. The first call evaluates config.cjs and stores its module.exports; the second call returns the same object without running the file again. a and b are therefore the same reference (true), and mutating b.mode is visible through a. This is why singletons and shared config work in CommonJS — and why tests must clear the require cache (or use dependency injection) when they need a fresh module.

Deleting require.cache[require.resolve("./config.cjs")] would force the next require to re-evaluate. ESM has the same one-instance rule, but the cache is not exposed for manual clearing.
key_points: require caches by resolved filename
The module body runs once
Repeated requires return the same object
Mutating the export is visible to all holders

questions.answer:
It throws ReferenceError: Cannot access 'aName' before initialization.

Node starts evaluating a.js, which imports b.js. b.js imports a.js, which is already in progress, so the module graph does not loop forever and b.js gets a live binding to aName. But a.js has not executed its const aName = "A" line yet, so the binding is still in its temporal dead zone. b.js reads it at the top level in console.log(aName), which throws.

If b.js only read aName later inside a function that runs after both modules finish, the cycle would work — the binding would be initialized by then. The same cycle is less obvious in CommonJS because require returns a partial module.exports instead of throwing, often yielding undefined. Fix cycles by extracting shared values into a third module or inverting the dependency.
key_points: ESM handles cycles through live bindings, not by duplicating modules
Uninitialized const/let bindings are in the TDZ
Reading the binding at top level during the cycle throws ReferenceError
Reading it later inside a function can work
